baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Studies nativism and ethnic relations as central to American nationalism and pluralism.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Dorothy Ross’s substantive retrospective describes the project and later revisions; the nativism interpretation is not an endorsement of exclusion.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Criticizes consensus narratives that flatten conflict and diversity in American history.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Existing complete1959primary reading, with original qualifications preserved; does not imply a wholesale return to older economic dualisms.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Uses Higham’s history of the profession to document American historians’ recovery of intellectual confidence after1945.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In the published address associated with1969 delivery, Woodward names Higham’s1965 account and quotes its diagnosis of restored professional self-respect. Notes1/11 credit Higham et al.; Leonard Krieger and Felix Gilbert retain their coauthor credit. The complete1965 book remains unread here; this is a specified historiographical resource, not an exclusive lineage.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Rodgers draws on Higham’s account of Protestant social-gospel thinking as one resource for explaining progressive languages of social bonds.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own1982 essay126 and note55 explicitly use this resource alongside Robert M.Crunden,Joseph F.Kett and Clyde Griffen,whose separate credit remains essential. Rodgers leaves the transatlantic reconstruction and channels of transmission open;this does not attribute the whole three-language synthesis to Higham. Higham’s original1974 article was not freshly read.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Bederman uses Higham’s accounts of nativism and cultural reorientation as resources for connecting white middle-class manhood to immigrant politics and the appeal of boxing.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Body13/n50 links immigrant contests for city government to power and manhood, citing Strangers in the Land (1971 consulted edition) with Gossett. Body17/n72 cites Reorientation,78–79 for boxing’s wider middle-class attraction. This scoped use coexists with her criticism of a masculinity-crisis formulation; it is not evidence of complete agreement. Originals unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Bederman qualifies the masculinity-crisis interpretation represented in part by Higham, arguing that ongoing change and contradictory authority claims do not by themselves establish a crisis of male identity or power.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Body10–11 acknowledges merit in both crisis and domesticity interpretations, then distinguishes remaking gender from evidence that men lost confidence in male identity and authority. Note36 names Higham’s Reorientation alongside Dubbert, Filene, Kimmel and McGovern; note37 credits Marsh and Griffen’s corrective. A bounded collective criticism, not rejection of all Higham’s work; her separate uses of his nativism and boxing discussions remain.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Treats Strangers in the Land as an important account of racial nativism from which to extend the study of immigration law.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, calls Higham's 1955 book the richest account, then identifies limits in treating the passage of restriction as the end of the story. This positive starting point coexists with her particular criticism. The reprinted acknowledgment, p. xvi, also includes Higham among scholarly helpers without assigning him an individual task. His original book remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Questions the limits of Higham’s nativism framework and its economic-downturn explanation of restriction.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, appreciates the classic account while arguing that legislative triumph narratives can obscure categories produced after enactment. The 2024 article treats eugenics as one cause and argues that nativist surges accompany structural change even during expansion, rather than simply cyclical downturns. Benton-Cohen retains credit for the Dillingham finding. This does not certify every historical example or refute Higham's entire work; the original books remain unread.
